Tokyo put 204 films inside ten days.

The 39th Tokyo International Film Festival entered its second day with 31 screenings. Its bigger argument is not the total: animation in Tokyo now means Japanese premieres, international work and the people who make moving images.

By Yuji Shimizu · YUJI @ Japan
Published October 27, 2026 at 12:15 JST · 7 min read

Tokyo’s cinema district woke up Tuesday with an impossible menu. The festival calendar listed 31 screenings for October 27, moving between Hibiya, Yurakucho and nearby theaters from morning into the night. One ticket could lead to a Japanese classic; the next, a world premiere or a film that had crossed continents before reaching Japan.

The 39th Tokyo International Film Festival runs from October 26 through November 4. Its official count is 204 films, up from 184 last year, representing 112 countries and regions. Eighty-three titles are Japanese, 35 are world premieres, and 47 films were directed or co-directed by women. Those figures describe scale, but not the shape of the program.

204films over ten festival days
112countries and regions represented
35world premieres in the lineup

The revealing number is nine: the festival’s Animation section contains nine new works, but it refuses to treat “animation” as another word for “Japanese anime.” It places Japanese features beside Brazilian, French and other international films—and adds a documentary about more than 70 animation makers.

One Japanese debut, thirty years of friendship

On Tuesday’s schedule, We Are Aliens gives the animation program a distinctly local doorway. The film is Kohei Kadowaki’s first feature as director and follows two boys across three decades of friendship. Ryota Bando and Amane Okayama lead the voice cast; NOTHING NEW and TOHO NEXT handle distribution.

The festival describes the film as youth nostalgia that drew attention at Cannes. That label can sound small beside aliens, futures and fantasy elsewhere in the lineup, but duration is its special effect. Thirty years allow childhood misunderstanding to become adult memory. The alien idea turns estrangement into an image rather than a lecture.

Other Japanese selections stretch in different directions. Ghost — End of Night is Shingo Natsume’s first original animated feature, made at Madhouse, about a young woman searching for something real in a future where labor is no longer necessary. Atsushi Nishigori and CloverWorks begin the collection Grotesqqque with aliens, a gyaru and a vampire. Masanao Kawajiri’s Cherry and Virgin pairs an adult-manga artist with a woman who loves boys’ love fiction.

The border around animation moved

The international entries complicate the familiar map. Brazil’s Amadeo and the Hypothetical New World imagines an African genius inventing photography in a nineteenth-century Brazil still structured by slavery. France’s Iron Boy, directed by Louis Clichy, follows a ten-year-old required to wear an iron corset; it arrived after winning three awards at the 2026 Annecy International Animation Film Festival.

Son of a Bitch sends a young man away from the brothel run by his mother and toward a father he has never met. DreamWorks’ Forgotten Island asks whether returning to reality is worth losing memories of a friend. The section therefore moves from intimate bodies to invented histories and global studio mythmaking without insisting on a single national style.

Then Walking with Animators changes the object of attention. Directors Alexandre Poncet and Gilles Penso spent eight years interviewing more than 70 artists and animators. Instead of presenting animation only as a finished screen illusion, the documentary brings labor, tools and creative choices into view.

Official 39th Tokyo International Film Festival trailer, published by TIFF. It contains footage from the actual 2026 lineup, including the opening, centerpiece and gala selections.

Old films are not outside the conversation

The program also returns to three features by women directors: Tomoka Nagaoka’s Detective Conan: The Fist of Blue Sapphire, Kotono Watanabe’s Gold Kingdom and Water Kingdom, and Ai Yoshimura’s theatrical The Rose of Versailles. These are not presented as novelty exceptions. Together they form a themed look at distinct worlds built inside commercial Japanese animation.

The Conan film moved the long-running detective franchise to Singapore and was its first theatrical entry directed by a woman. Gold Kingdom and Water Kingdom adapts Nao Iwamoto’s manga, which topped the women’s list in the 2017 edition of Kono Manga ga Sugoi!. The Rose of Versailles carries Riyoko Ikeda’s enormously influential manga about love, gender and power in revolutionary France into MAPPA’s 2025 film.

Putting those works beside new international features makes history active. Viewers can ask how studio systems, genre expectations and the meaning of authorship change across projects. A retrospective does not have to be a sealed room behind the new releases.

The festival is also a market

TIFF’s public screenings are only half the machinery. TIFFCOM, the associated content market, runs October 28–30 in Hamamatsucho. The festival says 24 film and animation projects will seek co-production and gap financing through the Tokyo Gap-Financing Market, while a Tokyo IP Market matches adaptation and remake rights with buyers.

That makes Tokyo both a viewing city and a deal-making city. A film can be art, a national cultural export, a package of territorial rights and the beginning of a remake conversation at the same time. The festival’s new leadership says it wants to bring world cinema into Japan while helping Japanese cinema travel outward.

The tension is useful. International attention on Japanese animation creates opportunity, but also pressure to repeat recognizable visual formulas. The broad animation selection argues that export strength can coexist with formal risk and work from outside Japan. Its most global gesture is not a Japanese title sent abroad; it is Tokyo creating a room where different animation traditions meet.

How to read the numbers

Two hundred and four films is a programming total, not a claim that any visitor can see everything. Thirty-one screenings on Tuesday overlap. Tickets, venues, subtitles and travel time decide what is practically available. The official schedule should be checked directly because event times and guest appearances can change.

Today’s Japanese word is 上映—じょうえい, jōei—a screening or the act of showing a film. 上 means “up” or “on,” and 映 means “project” or “reflect.” A natural announcement is 映画は午後一時から上映されます: “The film will be screened from 1 p.m.” It is a cinema and event word, more specific than simply “watch.”

The 204-film number gets attention. The better reason to follow the festival is the collision it makes possible: a restored classic after breakfast, a first feature after lunch, an animation that traveled through Annecy, and an industry meeting preparing the next film before this year’s audience has left the theater.
